Based on the retrieved matches, it appears that pectins play a role in both cold acclimation and de-acclimation of winter oil-seed rape plants. The information can be synthesized as follows:

Cold acclimation is a process where plants adapt to changing temperatures, and pectin content and its methyl esterification degree have been correlated with changes in tissue tensile strength, leaf expansion ability, and resistance to freezing.

During cold acclimation, pectins help to maintain the structural integrity of plant tissues by providing mechanical support and facilitating cell wall modification. This is evident from studies showing that temperature-dependent modifications in pectin content and their methyl esterification degree correlate with changes in tensile strength of a leaf tissue.

De-acclimation, on the other hand, refers to the process of plants returning to their normal growth conditions after exposure to cold temperatures. Pectins may also play a role in this process by helping to maintain cell wall integrity and support plant cell expansion during periods of stress.

Therefore, it can be concluded that pectins are involved in both cold acclimation and de-acclimation of winter oil-seed rape plants, highlighting their importance in maintaining plant tissue structure and function under changing environmental conditions.
